bugs: CustomerOrderController.php:14-16 only sorts by created_at with no tie-breaker. Orders with the same created_at (common after bulk imports) can appear on two pages or be skipped across paginate(50) pages on this busy endpoint.
antipatterns: app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:27 builds the SET subquery as DB::raw('('.$builder->toSql().')'). This drops any bindings, and the query builder already accepts a Builder as an update() value.

app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:22 always scans from id 1 to max(id). Each re-run walks the whole 20M-row range (about 4000 statements) instead of starting at the first unlinked id, so it is re-runnable but not resumable.

database/migrations/2026_11_07_200004_add_customer_foreign_key_to_orders_table.php:28-43 hand-writes a MySQL-only withoutForeignKeyChecks helper, which duplicates Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints().
app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:38 uses select(DB::raw('1')) and then overrides it with select('customers.id') at line 27, which is confusing reuse of one builder.
tests/Feature/CustomerOrdersTest.php:18-23 has a setUp that calls Http::preventStrayRequests() although nothing makes HTTP calls. It is noise.
Splitting the two indexes into two separate migrations (200002 and 200003) adds ceremony without benefit.
strengths: Migrations are ordered correctly: nullable column, then indexes, then the FK. The FK reuses the existing index, and nullOnDelete keeps orders when a customer is deleted.
Foreign key checks are turned off while adding the FK, so MySQL can add it in place instead of copying the table. A short comment explains why.
The backfill uses chunked set-based UPDATE ... WHERE customer_id IS NULL AND EXISTS(...) with the query builder, so updated_at is untouched and unmatched orders are left alone.
Implements Isolatable, which prevents two backfill runs at once. That is a good touch.
Both composite indexes fit the endpoint, with and without the status filter.
PlaceOrder uses $customer->orders()->create(), and the endpoint uses the relationship.

antipatterns: app/Console/Commands/LinkOrdersToCustomers.php:44-45 calls ->toBase() on $match even though whereExists and update already accept an Eloquent builder. It is redundant.
app/Http/Requests/IndexCustomerOrdersRequest.php adds a FormRequest for a single optional status string. That is slightly more ceremony than the task asked for, though it is defensible.
tests/Feature/LinkOrdersToCustomersTest.php:135 calls Http::preventStrayRequests() in a test that makes no HTTP calls. It is noise.

database/migrations/2026_11_07_200000_add_customer_id_to_orders_table.php:12 uses ->after('id'). MySQL can only add a column mid-table instantly from 8.0.29, so appending it at the end would be safer on older 8.0 patch releases.
strengths: Migrations are ordered as add nullable column, then the indexes in one ALTER, then the FK. nullOnDelete gives the required GDPR detach behaviour.
Uses the framework's Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints() so MySQL adds the FK in place without a validation scan, with a short comment explaining why.

The backfill uses the native Query Builder subquery update (update(['customer_id' => $builder])). It is set-based, chunked by id range, uses toBase() so updated_at is not bumped, and checks whereNull plus whereExists, so it is idempotent and leaves unmatched orders alone.
The backfill starts at min(id) of unlinked orders, which the customer_id index answers cheaply, so a re-run resumes near where the last run stopped.

The endpoint adds a latest('id') tie-breaker for stable pagination. The (customer_id, created_at) and (customer_id, status, created_at) indexes cover both query shapes, and InnoDB's implicit PK suffix covers the id tie-breaker.

Thorough tests cover several chunks, re-runs reporting 0 linked, keeping existing links, unmatched orders, updated_at being preserved, the indexes existing, linking by id rather than email, pagination order, auth/404 and validation.

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first and impl-1 second. Both suites pass (impl-2: 18 tests, impl-1: 11). Neither has a correctness flaw in the parts that matter most, and neither looks like a likely production incident.

What they share:
- **Migrations:** both add the column, then the indexes, then the FK in the right order, use nullOnDelete, and turn off foreign key checks so MySQL adds the FK in place.
- **Backfill:** both run chunked, set-based query-builder UPDATEs filtered by whereNull and EXISTS.
- **Probes:** both handled sparse ids, an unmatched order holding the lowest id, preserving updated_at, re-running after a customer is deleted, and `?status=` sent empty.

Why impl-2 ranks higher:
- **Framework APIs:** it uses the built-in ones, Schema::withoutForeignKeyConstraints and a Builder passed straight into update(). I checked in vendor that the installed version supports the latter. impl-1 hand-writes a MySQL-only FK-check helper and builds the subquery from toSql(), which silently drops any bindings.
- **Resuming the backfill:** impl-2 starts at the lowest unlinked id. impl-1 rescans ids 1 to max(id) on every run, about 4000 statements on a 20M-row table.
- **Pagination:** impl-2 adds an id tie-breaker. impl-1 can repeat or skip orders across pages on this busy endpoint when several share the same created_at.
- **Tests:** impl-2's are clearly broader, covering several chunks, the re-run count, the indexes, and pagination order and validation.

impl-1's one clear advantage is Isolatable, which stops two backfill runs at once. impl-2's FormRequest is a little more ceremony than needed, but it isn't harmful.
